digest.top_line: RSS SRS guideline: up to 15 lesions, ≤3 cm and ≤14 cc, are SRS-suitable. Fractionate 2-4 cm lesions (27 Gy/3 fx or 30 Gy/5 fx); above 4 cm, surgery first.
digest.tldr: CNS carried the day: RSS and ISRS SRS guidelines both require planning MRI ≤7 days pre-SRS, each resting on largely observational or single-institution evidence. ASTRO think tank: germline DNA-repair variants should not alter indicated RT, except young deleterious ATM carriers. Breast: consecutive-day 30 Gy/5 fx VMAT PBI (N=50) shows G1-only toxicity at median 4.5 yr.

studies.name: Implications of Genetic Testing on Radiation Therapy Decisions
studies.tldr: ASTRO think tank consensus: heterozygous germline DNA-repair variants (BRCA1/2, PALB2, CHEK2, RAD50) and VUS should not alter indicated RT; young deleterious ATM carriers are the exception.
details: 🔍 ASTRO think tank, Feb 2019: genetic screening, genomics, radiosensitivity, risk-estimate and clinical oncology experts

rows: Not actionable; RT risks similar to normal
Consistent data: no excess toxicity or RT-induced second cancers
Avoid optional RT in young pts; close CBC screening after indicated RT
Possible RT-attributable CBC excess; toxicity data mixed
No known excess acute or late toxicity

details: 📊 VUS can be found in >50% of multigene panel results

details.text: 📊 ATM carrier CBC risk, worked absolute-risk example (Box 3)
subdetails: Adjusted RR 1.3 for contralateral breast cancer (Women's Environment, Cancer, and Radiation Epidemiology study)
5-yr second breast cancer risk 2.9% (SEER) → estimated 3.8% in ATM carriers
Excess absolute risk 0.9% at 5 yrs

details: 📊 647,672 adult 5-yr survivors: 9% second solid malignancy, only 8% attributed to RT
📊 RT-attributable excess absolute risk of second solid malignancy 0.5% by 15 yrs
📊 Hereditary retinoblastoma: 30-yr second cancer incidence 35% with EBRT vs 6% without RT
📊 ATM SNP rs1801516 in ~24% of 5456 breast/prostate pts: OR 1.5 acute, 1.2 late toxicity; not actionable
📊 Paired tumor-normal sequencing: 17% pathogenic germline variants in 1040 advanced cancers; 101 of 182 missed by standard screening
📊 Somatic ATM truncation tracked with better local control after palliative RT vs VUS/wildtype (P < .001); OS no different
⚠️ Consensus reached by expert discussion; no voting, agreement rates or evidence grading reported
⚠️ Panel concedes heterozygous ATM toxicity data are evenly split for and against excess risk
⚠️ PALB2/CHEK2/RAD50 reassurance rests on BRCA analogy, not direct RT outcome data
studies.significance: The ATM carve-out is smaller than it sounds: an RR of 1.3 moves 5-yr contralateral breast cancer risk from 2.9% to an estimated 3.8%, and the panel calls toxicity data evenly split. Indicated RT in young ATM carriers still goes ahead with close CBC screening. Optional RT, such as omission-eligible adjuvant breast RT, is the decision this sharpens.
studies.monday_clinic: In a BRCA1/2, PALB2, CHEK2 or RAD50 carrier, or a pt with only a VUS, this consensus supports offering indicated RT unchanged; it does not cover recognized radiosensitivity syndromes such as ataxia telangiectasia or Li-Fraumeni.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: ASTRO-convened **think tank, February 2019**, of physicians and scientists in genetic screening, genomics, radiosensitivity, risk estimation and clinical oncology. Narrative review with consensus points; no voting or agreement metrics reported.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Addresses pts with **germline or somatic variants** found on hereditary screening, direct-to-consumer CLIA testing, or tumor genomic panels. Panel recommends only **CLIA-certified tests** inform RT discussion and prefers paired tumor-normal sequencing.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **VUS = normal.** **BRCA1/2: no excess RT toxicity or RT-induced second cancers**, extended to PALB2, CHEK2, RAD50. **Deleterious heterozygous ATM:** avoid optional RT in young pts, close CBC screening after indicated RT. RB1, NF1, TP53, PTCH1 syndromes carry elevated in-field second malignancy risk.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Somatic ATM truncation tracked with improved local control after palliative RT (**P < .001**) without OS difference, read as an RT-specific effect. No tumor mutation is yet **clinically actionable** for dose.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: NCCN guidance covers counseling for common germline mutations but gives little RT-specific risk information. REQUITE (~4400 pts, 8 countries) and the Radiogenomics Consortium are named as the routes to validated polygenic toxicity predictors.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents adults with heterozygous germline DNA-repair variants or VUS for whom RT is clinically indicated. Does not represent rare radiosensitivity syndromes such as ataxia telangiectasia or Li-Fraumeni, which carry distinct risks.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The ATM absolute risk is a rough estimate built from a SEER baseline and one cohort's RR, not a measured carrier-specific rate. Most cited studies lack a no-RT control, so RT-attributable risk is often inferred.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Panel proposes future genomic-adjusted RT trials include a **no-RT arm** to separate prognostic from predictive value. Polygenic, not single-gene, predictors are expected to be what eventually becomes actionable.

studies.interpretation:
The document's main contribution is a default. A heterozygous germline hit in a DNA-repair gene is not, on its own, a reason to change an indicated RT plan. That default rests on uneven footing. For BRCA1/2 the panel cites consistent clinical data showing no excess toxicity or RT-induced second cancers with standard adjuvant regimens, and this is the firmest ground in the paper. PALB2, CHEK2 and RAD50 are then brought under the same umbrella as phenotypically similar heterozygous repair variants, by analogy rather than from direct outcome data. A reader should keep those two tiers separate: the first is measured, the second is reasoned.

ATM is where the paper earns its carve-out, and where its evidence is thinnest. The panel concedes that data on heterozygous ATM and toxicity cut both ways about equally, yet still recommends avoiding optional RT in young carriers. The justification is the contralateral breast cancer signal plus the age gradient of radiation carcinogenesis, not toxicity. The Box 3 arithmetic is the most usable counseling tool in the paper: a relative risk of 1.3 becomes a 5-year move from 2.9% to roughly 3.8%. That figure joins a population baseline to one cohort's relative risk, so it is an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a carrier-specific measurement, and should be presented to pts that way.

The second load-bearing idea is the line between syndromic and incidental findings. The rare syndromes in Table 1 carry real in-field second malignancy risk; hereditary retinoblastoma, with 30-year second cancers of 35% after EBRT vs 6% without RT, shows the stakes. The panel argues these syndromes usually declare themselves in childhood, so an adult panel result is unlikely to be one. The exception it flags is paired tumor-normal sequencing, which surfaces occult TP53 carriers in otherwise low-risk pts. That is the setting where an adult finding deserves a closer look before RT.

The somatic material is more speculative but more relevant to dose. Truncating somatic ATM mutations tracked with better local control after palliative RT with no OS difference, which reads as an RT-specific effect. Still, the panel itself states no tumor mutation is clinically actionable, and its proposed trial design, with a no-RT arm to separate prognostic from predictive value, is the right bar for any future genomic dose-adjustment claim.

What would overturn this? A large prospective toxicity dataset such as REQUITE showing a clinically meaningful excess for a specific heterozygous variant. The consensus process is also undocumented: no votes, agreement rates or evidence grades are reported, so this carries the weight of expert opinion from a 2019 convening. Of its conclusions, the BRCA position is least likely to move; the ATM recommendation is most exposed to new data in either direction.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The ATM carve-out is smaller than it sounds: an RR of 1.3 moves 5-yr contralateral breast cancer risk from 2.9% to an estimated 3.8%, and toxicity data are evenly split. Indicated RT still goes ahead with close CBC screening; optional RT in young ATM carriers is the decision this sharpens.

open_questions: Does heterozygous ATM truly raise RT toxicity risk?
Validated polygenic risk score for radiation toxicity
Genomic-adjusted RT dose tested against a no-RT arm

sites.intro: Two SRS guidelines. The ISRS panel reached strong consensus on only 5 of 10 survey questions, and RSS states no panel process.

studies.name: ISRS Technical Guidelines: SRS for Small Brain Metastases (≤1 cm)
studies.tldr: Sub-mm geometric accuracy, ≤1 mm E2E tolerance, 5% dosimetric accuracy and MRI ≤7 days pre-SRS anchor ISRS physics consensus for ≤1 cm brain mets.
details: 🔍 PRISMA systematic review of PubMed 2009-2020: 484 abstracts → 37 articles, plus 44 from references
⚠️ Evidence base thin: 57 of 81 papers (70%) single-institution
🔍 14-member ISRS committee survey, 10 questions: strong consensus (≥80%) on only 5, none on 3

rows: MRI ≤7 days from treatment is a prerequisite for contouring
Fine-cut MR, ≤1.5-mm slices; planning CT no thicker than MR slices
10 to 15 min scan delay after contrast injection
SRS-optimized sequences; regular MRI QA for geometric distortion
Contour all targets and OARs; weigh margins per SRS platform
Sub-mm geometric accuracy; immobilization and IGRT chosen to achieve it
Lower energy beams may reduce normal tissue dose
Dosimetric accuracy within 5%; small-field dosimetry per IAEA and AAPM

details.text: 🔗 Margin evidence cited by the panel

rows: No LC difference; more radionecrosis with 3 mm
Severe parenchymal complications 7.1% and 19.6%; no LC effect
Necrosis risk up 6% to 25%; only 1 of 15 lesions <1 cm

details: 📐 1-mm margin on a 0.8-cm sphere: 0.268 → 0.524 cc, effectively doubling target volume
📊 Planning MRI <14 vs ≥14 days before SRS: 12-mo local FFP 95% vs 56% (retrospective, 151 mets)
📐 Median 20% tumor volume growth over a median 8-day interscan interval (531 lesions)
📊 Dose for 1 cm lesions in practice ranges 18 to 25 Gy; guideline sets no prescription

subdetails: MLC ≤5 mm width a prerequisite; 2.5 vs 5 mm superiority not settled
6 MV FFF: 50% isodose volume 11% lower than 10 MV FFF (93 lesions, 35 pts)
Single-isocenter VMAT: uncertainty within 1 mm ≤4 cm from isocenter, 2 mm beyond
Dedicated SRS mask: median 0.38 mm displacement (max 1 mm) vs 0.74 mm (max 2 mm) conventional mask
Without real-time monitoring, imaging-to-beam-on delay preferably under 5 min

details: ⚠️ Multiple authors disclose Elekta, BrainLAB, Accuray or Varian ties; no specific funding
studies.significance: The margin is the lever on these targets: a 1-mm expansion takes a 0.8-cm met from 0.268 to 0.524 cc, and the one randomized comparison (1 vs 3 mm, 80 mets) showed no LC difference with more radionecrosis at 3 mm. Planning-MRI age also gates control: 12-mo local FFP 95% vs 56% at <14 vs ≥14 days.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: ISRS physics guideline built on a **PRISMA systematic review** of PubMed 2009-2020 (81 papers plus 7 international guidelines) and a **10-question survey** of 14 committee members, 100% completion.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Scope is SRS for brain metastases **≤1 cm in maximal diameter** on Gamma Knife, CyberKnife and SRS-adapted LINACs. Platform mix of included papers: LINAC 21, mixed 21, GK 20, CK 2.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Requires **sub-mm geometric accuracy**, a **≤1 mm** geometric tolerance on system-specific E2E tests, and **dosimetric accuracy within 5%**. MLC width of no more than 5 mm is called a prerequisite; no CTV margin is usually applied, and PTV margin use is left platform-dependent.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Defers small-field dosimetry and QA tolerances to **AAPM TG142, TG198 and TG178** and **IAEA TRS 483**, and adopts the **ICRU 91** GTV definition. The ISRS contribution is the small-target layer: imaging recency, slice thickness, contrast timing and margin trade-offs.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents SRS programs treating brain metastases ≤1 cm on GK, CK or adapted LINACs. Does not represent lesions >1 cm, dose selection, or cumulative normal-brain dose from repeat SRS.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Survey reached **no consensus on 3 of 10 questions**, so several statements reflect unresolved practice variation. Commissioning, QA program design and platform-specific planning are explicitly out of scope, and several authors carry vendor ties.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The panel frames **margin addition or omission as the most controversial variable** for small mets: absolute necrosis risk at this size is low, so relative increases may matter less in absolute terms. Cumulative dose across repeat SRS sessions is flagged as an open, clinically relevant problem.

studies.interpretation:
This is a physics document, and it should be read as one. It does not tell a radiation oncologist what dose to give a 7-mm melanoma metastasis or whether to treat it at all; it tells a program what has to be true about its imaging, contouring, immobilization and dosimetry chain before a sub-centimetre target can be treated with confidence. Its value is in compressing a scattered technical literature into a short list of conditions, and in naming where the field has not converged.

The evidence underneath the recommendations is uneven. Of 81 included papers, 57 were single-institution, and the clinical outcome data on margins rest on a handful of studies: one randomized comparison of 1 vs 3 mm PTV margins in 49 pts with 80 mets, a retrospective series of 93 mets, Sneed's Gamma Knife experience of 2200 treatments, and a modeling exercise by Ma et al in which only 1 of 15 lesions was under 1 cm. The randomized trial found no local control difference and more radionecrosis at 3 mm, which supports keeping margins small, but it does not test zero against 1 mm, which is the decision most LINAC programs actually face. The committee's own survey reflects that gap: strong consensus on 5 of 10 questions and none on 3.

The most practice-relevant numbers concern time and geometry rather than dose. A planning MRI 14 or more days old was associated with 12-mo local freedom from progression of 56% against 95% for fresher imaging, and a separate series measured median volume growth of 20% over a median 8-day interval. Both are retrospective, but the direction is mechanistically plausible and the cost of acting on it is low, which is why the ≤7-day imaging recommendation is likely the easiest to adopt. The volume arithmetic for margins is similarly hard to argue with: a 1-mm expansion of a 0.8-cm sphere roughly doubles the treated volume, which for multiple adjacent mets compounds normal-brain dose.

Relative to the AAPM task group reports and IAEA TRS 483, which the document leans on rather than replaces, the ISRS contribution is specificity to target size. The single-isocenter data are a good example: uncertainty within 1 mm inside 4 cm of isocenter and 2 mm beyond is exactly the kind of figure a program treating many small mets with one isocenter needs to weigh when deciding whether a peripheral target needs its own plan or a margin.

What would make the guideline wrong is mostly what it does not measure. If penumbral dose or immune effects compensate for small geometric misses, as the authors speculate, then the sub-mm insistence may be stricter than outcomes require; if cumulative dose across repeat SRS courses proves to drive late toxicity, the single-session framing will understate risk. Vendor ties among several authors are disclosed and worth noting, though the recommendations are largely platform-neutral.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The margin is the lever on these targets: a 1-mm expansion takes a 0.8-cm met from 0.268 to 0.524 cc, and the one randomized comparison (1 vs 3 mm) showed no LC difference with more radionecrosis at 3 mm. Planning-MRI age also gates control: 12-mo local FFP 95% vs 56% at <14 vs ≥14 days.

open_questions: Does no margin vs 1 mm PTV margin change LC for ≤1 cm mets?
Cumulative normal-brain dose limits across repeat SRS courses
Does 2.5 vs 5 mm MLC width change outcomes for small targets?

studies.name: Case-Based Radiosurgery Society Practice Guideline: SRS for Brain Metastases
studies.tldr: Up to 15 lesions, ≤3 cm and ≤14 cc are SRS-suitable. Fractionate 2-4 cm lesions (27 Gy/3 fx or 30 Gy/5 fx). Above 4 cm, surgery comes first.

rows: Diameter 3-6 cm, volume >14 cc (operative management preferred)
27 Gy in 3 fx or 30 Gy in 5 fx; staged SRS an alternative
Surgery; multifraction over single-fraction SRS if inoperable

details.text: 🔗 Cited meta-analysis (24 studies, 1887 lesions): single- vs multifraction SRS for large mets

details: 📊 Single-fraction V12 of 5, 10, >15 cc → symptomatic RN ~10%, 15%, 20% (HyTEC)
🔍 PTV margin 1-2 mm if one is used, 1 mm whenever possible
📐 Margin cost: V12 doubles going 0 → 1 mm and triples going 0 → 2 mm (48 plans)

subdetails: CTV: whole cavity on contrast T1, edema excluded
Up to 5 mm along meningeal margin / bone flap
Up to 10 mm along bone flap if tumor touched dura preop
1-5 mm along an abutting venous sinus
PTV typically 2 mm, 1 mm in select cases
SRS within 4 wk of surgery, planning MRI ≤7 days prior

details: 💊 Concurrent systemic therapy + SRS: no routine washout per most cited studies
⚠️ Exceptions flagged: BRAF inhibitors (intratumoral bleeding), erlotinib with WBRT + SRS (RN)
🔗 Preop SRS: meningeal disease 5.8% vs 16% to 21% postop, from initial studies only
⚠️ 15-lesion ceiling rests on an observational study and an early-terminated, abstract-only trial
⚠️ No panel process, evidence grading or agreement metric stated in source
studies.significance: The fractionation advice is driven by toxicity more than control. In 4-14 cc lesions, radionecrosis was 23.1% single-fraction vs 7.3% multifraction (P = .003). Above 14 cc and 3 cm, neither LC nor necrosis differed significantly, which is the guide's case for moving to surgery. Margin is the other lever: going from 0 to 2 mm triples V12.
studies.monday_clinic: In an intact 2-4 cm metastasis where resection is not an option, this supports 27 Gy/3 fx or 30 Gy/5 fx over single-fraction SRS. It does not extend to classical leptomeningeal disease or lesions >6 cm.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Case-based practice guideline** sponsored by the Radiosurgery Society, built around two cases: 7 NSCLC brain mets treated with 20 Gy/1 fx, and a resected 3.5 cm cerebellar colon met given 27 Gy/3 fx postop. The source states no panel voting, evidence grading or agreement metric.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Suitable:** 1-15 lesions, diameter ≤3 cm, volume ≤14 cc. **Cautionary:** >15 lesions, 3-6 cm or >14 cc, SCLC, nodular LMD. **Unsuitable:** >6 cm or classical LMD.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **<2 cm: 20-24 Gy/1 fx; 2-4 cm: 27 Gy/3 fx or 30 Gy/5 fx; >4 cm: surgery**, with multifraction SRS if inoperable. Intact-lesion target is GTV on contrast T1 with a **1-2 mm PTV (1 mm whenever possible)** and no CTV. Postop target is the cavity CTV with a PTV typically 2 mm, delivered within 4 wk of surgery.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Single-fraction brain V12 of 5, 10, >15 cc carries ~10%, 15%, 20% symptomatic RN. For reirradiation the guide cites total brain EQD2 <120 Gy, cumulative cord EQD2 ≤70 Gy and **at least 5 months** between courses.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The guide builds on RTOG 9508 (WBRT + SRS vs WBRT) and on N107C/RTOG 1270 in the postop setting, which made SRS alone standard for 1-4 mets. It extends SRS beyond that population to **up to 15 lesions**, larger lesions via fractionation, and preoperative SRS.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents adults with brain metastases being considered for SRS, intact or postoperative, including multiple lesions and select SCLC or nodular LMD. Does not represent classical leptomeningeal disease, lesions >6 cm, or primary CNS tumors.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The **15-lesion boundary** rests on a prospective observational study and an MD Anderson trial terminated early and published only as an abstract. The preop SRS LMD advantage comes from initial studies, and the guide itself reports similar LC, distant brain failure and OS for pre- and postoperative SRS.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Volume may matter more than count: on MVA, tumor volume, KPS and histology predicted OS but lesion number did not. Integral brain dose is offered as the practical ceiling, where a 9-, 177- or 42-tumor burden yields an 8 Gy whole-brain dose depending on size. The guide calls SRS in SCLC an acceptable option but not yet the default.

studies.interpretation:
This is a practice guide rather than a graded guideline: two cases, a suitability table, a dose-constraint table and narrative recommendations, with no stated panel process, evidence grading or agreement metric. Its value is in writing down what high-volume SRS programs already do. Its weak points sit where the field is moving fastest.

The lesion-count ceiling of 15 is the clearest example. The authors base it on a 2014 multi-institutional prospective observational study, which found 5 to 10 lesions (total volume <15 cc) noninferior to 2 to 4, and on an MD Anderson trial of SRS vs WBRT in 4 to 15 metastases that was terminated early and exists only as an abstract. That is a thin base for a hard 'suitable' boundary. The paper itself concedes that volume may outrank count, citing an MVA in which tumor volume, KPS and histology predicted OS while lesion number did not. A reader treating 12 small lesions and a reader treating 4 bulky ones should take more from the volume argument and the whole-brain dose estimate than from the number in Table 1.

The fractionation advice is better grounded, and its strongest data concern toxicity, not control. In the cited meta-analysis of 24 studies and 1887 lesions, multifraction SRS cut radionecrosis from 23.1% to 7.3% (P = .003) in 4-14 cc lesions. For the largest group, neither LC (77.1% vs 79.2%, P = .76) nor necrosis (11.7% vs 6.5%, P = .29) separated. That pattern supports the guide's move to surgery above 3 to 4 cm: fractionation buys safety in mid-size lesions but does not rescue control in the biggest ones. The HyTEC estimate of 1-year LC 69% to 75% single-fraction vs approximately 80% fractionated for 2.1 to 4 cm lesions points the same way.

The preoperative SRS section deserves the most caution. The 5.8% meningeal disease rate, against 16% to 21% postoperatively, comes from what the authors call initial studies. They also report that pre- and postoperative SRS have shown similar LC, distant brain failure, OS and need for salvage WBRT. The LMD advantage is a hypothesis for the ongoing prospective trials to test. Postoperative SRS remains the option with level 1 evidence, a point Table 3 makes explicitly.

The concurrent systemic therapy guidance (no routine washout) rests on a systematic review and retrospective series. BRAF inhibitors (intratumoral bleeding) and erlotinib given with WBRT plus SRS are the named exceptions. The survival gap of 41.6 vs 21.5 months with concurrent therapy is confounded by which patients were fit enough to receive it and should not be read as a treatment effect. Endorsing SRS in SCLC on a 9-study meta-analysis while declining to make it the default is the right calibration. Here the guide is candid that the prospective data are missing.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Fractionation is a toxicity lever: in 4-14 cc lesions, radionecrosis was 23.1% single-fraction vs 7.3% multifraction (P = .003). Margin is the other lever, since 0 → 2 mm triples V12. That is the basis for a 1 mm PTV whenever setup confidence allows.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Most cited studies support giving systemic therapy concurrently with SRS without a washout. BRAF inhibitors (intratumoral bleeding) and erlotinib with WBRT plus SRS are the flagged exceptions. Per ASCO-SNO-ASTRO, deferring SRS for asymptomatic mets on CNS-active therapy is a conditional, multidisciplinary call.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Resection is first-line above 4 cm. The size and volume thresholds (≤3 cm, ≤14 cc) mark where SRS alone stops being the default. Preop SRS reported 5.8% meningeal disease vs 16% to 21% postop, but only in initial studies, and LC, distant brain failure and OS were similar.

open_questions: Does preop SRS lower leptomeningeal disease vs postop SRS in prospective trials?
Role of SRS vs WBRT in SCLC brain metastases
SRS vs WBRT for more than 15 brain metastases

studies.name: Natural History of DCIS of the Breast
studies.tldr: 14–53% of DCIS misdiagnosed as benign and left after biopsy alone progressed to invasive cancer over 10+ yr; precise progression rates not estimable.
details: 📊 DCIS misdiagnosed as benign, biopsy only: 14–53% progressed to invasive cancer over 10+ yr

subdetails: Page: 28 misdiagnosed of 11,760; 7 invasive by 15 yr, 2 more at 23 and 31 yr
Eusebi: 80 misdiagnosed; 11 invasive after mean 17.5 yr f/u
Nurses' Health study: 6 of 13 invasive, 2 each low, intermediate, high grade
Betsill: low grade micropapillary; 7 of 10 with f/u developed cancer, mean 9.7 yr
Rosen: micropapillary; 8 of 15 with f/u invasive in same breast, mean 9 yr f/u

details.text: 📊 Boyages meta-analysis: DCIS recurrence by treatment and tumour feature

details: 📊 Long-term BCS series: up to 40% ipsilateral recurrence, about half as invasive cancer
📊 Autopsy: median undiagnosed DCIS prevalence 8.9% (range 0–14.7%) vs invasive 1.3%
🔍 Kopans model: DCIS reservoir up to 20 times detected count expected even if all DCIS progresses
⚠️ Misdiagnosed series mostly low grade; progression for high grade likely underestimated
⚠️ Incomplete f/u (Rosen: 15 of 30) may enrich for women later diagnosed with cancer
⚠️ Autopsy prevalence likely inflated by ADH/DCIS misclassification and non-representative decedents
studies.significance: The RT-relevant read is the recurrence gap: pooled recurrence 22.5% after CS alone vs 8.9% with CS+RT, widest for comedo type (34.4% vs 8.3%), with about half of recurrences invasive. Low-grade DCIS recurs with longer latency, so short follow-up flatters RT omission in exactly the lesions where omission is proposed.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Review drawing on MEDLINE and citation tracking of key reviews and editorials. Evidence streams: **misdiagnosed-DCIS follow-up**, recurrence after BCS, autopsy, risk factors, animal and mathematical models.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Untreated misdiagnosed DCIS progressed in **14–53%** over 10+ yr. Pooled recurrence **22.5%** CS alone, **8.9%** CS+RT, **1.4%** mastectomy. Autopsy median DCIS prevalence **8.9%**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Predates the low-risk DCIS active-surveillance trials (LORIS, COMET, LORD), which test directly the progression question this review could only estimate indirectly from misdiagnosed biopsies.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents the indirect evidence base on how often DCIS becomes invasive and how often it recurs after excision. Does not represent a randomized estimate of progression or of RT benefit by grade.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Recurrence after surgery **may not reflect the untreated course** and depends strongly on excision margins. Boyages subgroup rates are pooled across series, not randomized contrasts.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors conclude DCIS is a precursor of most invasive breast cancer but **not all DCIS progresses** in the medium term. The autopsy reservoir argument for overdiagnosis is weakened because modelling predicts that reservoir even if all DCIS progresses.

studies.interpretation:
The useful move in this review is that it separates two questions a DCIS discussion tends to blur: how often DCIS becomes invasive if left in place, and how often it returns after excision with or without RT. The misdiagnosed-biopsy series speak to the first, the Boyages pooled recurrence data to the second, and the authors are explicit that neither can stand in for the other. Recurrence after surgery describes residual disease shaped by margins, not the natural course of an untouched lesion.

The 14–53% progression range deserves less confidence than its frequent citation suggests. It comes from a handful of small retrospective series, the largest identifying 80 misdiagnosed cases, and the biases run in both directions. Most lesions were low grade, which pushes the estimate down for high-grade disease. Follow-up was incomplete in several series, half of Rosen's cohort for example, and women later diagnosed with cancer were easier to trace, which pushes it up. Latency matters too: in the Page series, two invasive cancers appeared at 23 and 31 years, so a 10 to 15 year window truncates the outcome for exactly the indolent lesions now proposed for de-escalation.

For an RT reader, the Boyages figures carry the decision content. Pooled recurrence after CS alone was 22.5% against 8.9% with CS+RT, and the absolute difference was largest for comedo type, necrosis, and high and intermediate nuclear grade. These are pooled rates across series with different margins and follow-up, not randomized subgroup contrasts, so they describe where RT appeared to do the most work rather than proving where it can be dropped. The review's own observation that low-grade DCIS recurs with longer latency is the more important point for omission: a low-grade cohort looks safe at short follow-up partly because its events have not happened yet.

The autopsy argument is handled more carefully than it usually is. A median undiagnosed DCIS prevalence of 8.9% is often read as proof of overdiagnosis, but the Kopans model shows a reservoir of that kind would exist even if every lesion eventually progressed, simply because slow growers sit below the detection threshold for years. Classification drift between ADH and DCIS further inflates the autopsy numbers. That leaves the overdiagnosis case resting mainly on the misdiagnosed-biopsy series, which are the weakest-sampled data in the review.

What this does not settle is grade-specific and age-specific progression, and which markers identify the lesion that will invade. The later active-surveillance trials (LORIS, COMET, LORD) were designed to answer the progression question prospectively in low-risk disease; this review explains why the retrospective literature could not, and why their follow-up will need to be long before a reassuring early result means much.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: CS+RT cut pooled recurrence to 8.9% from 22.5% with CS alone, with the largest gaps in comedo type, necrosis, and high and intermediate nuclear grade. These are cross-series pooled rates, not randomized subgroup contrasts, so they inform but do not settle RT omission by grade, especially for slow-recurring low-grade DCIS.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Recurrence depends strongly on excision margins, and pooled recurrence was 1.4% after mastectomy vs 22.5% after CS alone. DCIS left after biopsy alone progressed in 14–53% over 10+ yr, so incomplete excision is not a benign default, though most of those lesions were low grade.

studies.name: APBI-IMRT-Florence Technique Update (VMAT)
studies.tldr: 30 Gy/5 consecutive-fraction VMAT PBI, N=50: G1-only toxicity (acute 32%, late 16%) at median 4.5 yr f/u, no G>1 events.
details: 🔍 Single-center consecutive series, N=50 (39 left, 11 right), free breathing
🔍 Dosimetric planning guide plus RTOG/EORTC toxicity; parent trial NCT02104895

🔍 PTV may extend max 4 mm into lung, cropped 3 mm from skin

verdict.rationale: Single-center consecutive series, 50 pts, no comparator arm; toxicity and dosimetry only, no local control. Consecutive-day schedule never tested within the parent phase 3.
verdict.audience: Early breast cancer selected for PBI, postoperative

studies.significance: The PTV-to-ipsilateral-breast volume ratio predicts ipsilateral breast V15Gy (R2 .911), so a planner can tell before optimizing whether a pt will meet the V15Gy ≤50% constraint. Consecutive daily fractions gave numerically more G1 toxicity than the trial's alternate-day schedule (acute 32% vs 21.1%, late 16% vs 4.5%), none above G1.
studies.monday_clinic: In early breast cancer pts selected for PBI, this supports 30 Gy/5 on consecutive days as an alternative to every-other-day delivery; it does not extend to pts whose plan misses the acceptable OAR constraints, who go to WBI.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-center (University of Florence) report of **50 consecutive pts**, 39 left and 11 right-sided, with dosimetric analysis and RTOG/EORTC toxicity scoring. **No comparator arm.** Median follow-up **4.5 yr** (mean 3.4; range 0.6-5).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **30 Gy in 5 consecutive fractions** via partial-arc VMAT, free breathing, replacing five-field step-and-shoot IMRT on alternate days. CTV = clips + 1.5 cm, PTV = CTV + 0.5 cm, PTV up to 4 mm into lung and cropped 3 mm from skin. **A plan that misses the acceptable constraints goes to WBI.**

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Acute any-grade G1 toxicity in **32%** (dermatitis 28%), late G1 in **16%** (fibrosis 14%). **No G>1 event.** Physician cosmesis excellent 84%, good 14%, fair 2%.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The parent APBI-IMRT-Florence phase 3 trial showed no significant IBTR or survival difference vs WBI at 10 yr, with better toxicity and cosmesis. Against that trial this series reports **more G1 toxicity** (acute 32% vs 21.1%, late 16% vs 4.5%). FAST-Forward 26 Gy/5 WBI reported moderate or marked normal tissue effects in 11.9% at 5 yr but has not been tested within a PBI phase 3.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents early breast cancer pts selected for PBI whose plan meets the Florence constraints. Does not represent pts failing the acceptable constraints, who are moved to WBI.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Median follow-up of 4.5 yr is hard to square with VMAT adopted in the past 3 yr. Some pts had a 1-day weekend break, and the lung, heart and contralateral breast dosimetry comes from free-breathing plans at one center only.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The useful output is a **planning template**: the constraint set plus the volume-ratio predictor let a center screen candidates before optimizing. The authors note VMAT and inverse planning may be unavailable in low-income settings or hard to get insurance-authorized in the US, and cite planning work suggesting 3D-CRT is a feasible alternative.

studies.interpretation:
This is a technique paper, not an efficacy paper, and it should be read that way. Its clinical weight comes from the parent APBI-IMRT-Florence phase 3 trial, which reported no significant difference in ipsilateral breast tumor recurrence or survival vs WBI at 10 years, with better toxicity and cosmesis in the PBI arm. This report adds the move of that schedule into current practice: partial-arc VMAT in place of five-field step-and-shoot IMRT, and consecutive daily fractions in place of the alternate-day schedule the trial used. Neither change was tested inside the trial, so the oncologic results carry over only on an assumption: that dose, volumes and constraints drive the efficacy, and the delivery method and schedule do not.

The schedule change is the part a radiation oncologist should weigh most. The trial chose alternate days as a hedge against toxicity, and the authors' own comparison suggests removing that hedge had a cost: any-grade acute toxicity of 32% here vs 21.1% in the trial, and early late toxicity of 16% vs 4.5%. Every event was grade 1, and physician-rated cosmesis was good or excellent in 98%, so the absolute cost is small. Still, the direction fits a per-day dose effect, and a 50-patient series at this follow-up cannot rule out a late fibrosis or cosmesis gap that shows up only later. The external support the authors cite for consecutive delivery is the prone Shah et al series, which mixed alternate-day and consecutive treatment, so it is supportive rather than a direct test.

The FAST-Forward comparison is where the argument is strongest, and also where it needs the most care. FAST-Forward established 26 Gy in 5 fractions as noninferior to 40 Gy in 15 for whole-breast treatment, with moderate or marked clinician-assessed normal tissue effects in 11.9% of 26 Gy pts at 5 years. The two series grade toxicity on different scales (RTOG/EORTC grade here, clinician-assessed breast effects there), so their numbers should not be compared directly. A fair reading is that both 30 Gy/5 PBI and 26 Gy/5 WBI are defensible one-week options, and that the choice between them rests on target volume and pt selection. No head-to-head toxicity result exists.

For a planning team, the most portable finding is the near-linear relationship between the PTV-to-ipsilateral-breast volume ratio and ipsilateral breast V15Gy (R2 .911). It turns the V15Gy ≤50% constraint into a screen before planning starts: a large cavity in a small breast predicts a failed plan before anyone optimizes it, and the protocol's answer to a failed plan is WBI. That makes selection explicit. It also means the favorable toxicity belongs to pts whose anatomy already met the constraint. The relationship comes from one center's contours and free-breathing VMAT plans, so a center using prone positioning, different margins or 3D-CRT should check it against its own plans first.

The report leaves several questions open. It gives no recurrence data for this cohort, so it cannot show that consecutive delivery keeps the trial's 10-year local control. It cannot show whether the small toxicity excess grows with longer follow-up. And it cannot show that the results hold outside a center with VMAT access. The authors raise that last point themselves: inverse-planned IMRT and VMAT may be unavailable or hard to get authorized, and they cite planning work in which 3D-CRT met coverage goals with somewhat worse homogeneity.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The PTV-to-ipsilateral-breast volume ratio predicts ipsilateral breast V15Gy (R2 .911), which screens PBI candidates before planning. Consecutive daily 30 Gy/5 carried more G1 toxicity than alternate days (acute 32% vs 21.1%, late 16% vs 4.5%), all G1, so the schedule change costs little.

open_questions: Does consecutive-day delivery preserve the parent trial's 10-yr IBTR?
Does the G1 toxicity excess vs alternate-day delivery persist with longer f/u?
Can 3D-CRT meet the updated Florence constraints?
